{{Short description|Theorem in stochastic calculus}}
The '''Doob&ndash;Meyer decomposition theorem''' is a theorem in [[stochastic calculus]] stating the conditions under which a [[Martingale (probability theory)#Submartingales and supermartingales|submartingale]] may be decomposed in a unique way as the sum of a  [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] and an [[increasing process|increasing]] [[predictable process]]. It is named for [[Joseph L. Doob]] and [[Paul-André Meyer]].

==History==
In 1953, Doob published the [[Doob decomposition theorem]] which gives a unique decomposition for certain discrete time martingales.<ref>Doob 1953</ref> He conjectured a continuous time version of the theorem and in two publications in 1962 and 1963 [[Paul-André Meyer]] proved such a theorem, which became known as the Doob-Meyer decomposition.<ref>Meyer 1962</ref><ref>Meyer 1963</ref> In honor of Doob, Meyer used the term "class D" to refer to the class of supermartingales for which his unique decomposition theorem applied.<ref>Protter 2005</ref>

==Class D supermartingales==
A [[càdlàg]] [[Martingale_(probability_theory)#Submartingales_and_supermartingales|supermartingale]] <math> Z </math> is of Class D if <math>Z_0=0</math> and the collection
:<math> \{Z_T \mid T \text{ a finite-valued stopping time} \} </math>
is [[uniform integrability|uniformly integrable]].<ref name="Protter">Protter (2005)</ref>

== Theorem ==
Let <math>(\Omega, \mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}, \mathbb{P})</math> be a filtered probability space satisfying the usual conditions (i.e. the filtration is right-continuous and complete; see [[Filtration (probability theory)]]). If <math>X = (X_t)_{t\ge0}</math> is a right-continuous submartingale of class D, then there exist unique adapted processes <math>M</math> and <math>A</math> such that
:<math> X_t = M_t + A_t, \qquad t \ge 0,
</math>
where
* <math>M</math> is a uniformly integrable martingale,
* <math>A</math> is a [[Predictable process|predictable]], right-continuous, increasing process with <math>A_0 = 0</math>.
The decomposition <math>(M, A)</math> is unique up to indistinguishability.

''Remark''. For a class D supermartingale, the process A is integrable and of finite variation on bounded intervals.<ref name="KaratzasShreve">Karatzas &amp; Shreve (1991), Theorem&nbsp;4.10.</ref>
